title: Are we in ‘the jackpot’? Will we die? | CNN
text:
Source: CNN

As one crucial computer system after another failed in the past week — triggering the global Microsoft outage, followed by the Federal Aviation Administration’s nationwide ground stop, followed by more outages and glitches hitting Workday,Chase Bank,United Airlines, theNational Security Agency’sinternal communications system, Apple — many people hadparticular fearsabout what might be going on: Was this a string of cyberattacks? Was it the result of pushing too much AI too fast?

Other people, watching the disruptions snowball, had a broader, even more menacing question: Was this the jackpot?

“Are we, uh, living through the jackpot right now,” oneBlueskyuser wrote. “FML this feels like the Jackpot,” saidanother.

“The jackpot” is a term coined by the science fiction novelist William Gibson in 2014, in his novel “The Peripheral.” Gibson — who decades ago looked at the oncoming future and invented the term “cyberspace” — came up with “the jackpot” as a term for a particular, ever-more-plausible kind of 21st century apocalypse.

EDITOR’S NOTE:CNN’s “Word of the Week” brings you the meaning behind the words in the news.

In “The Peripheral” and the rest of Gibson’s Jackpot Trilogy, 80% of humanity has been wiped out — but not as the result of some singular, world-shattering event like a nuclear war or the outbreak of some incurably deadly pathogen. Instead, civilization has collapsed from a set of intersecting environmental, economic and political crises that unfold gradually over time.

As one of his characters explains, the jackpot “was multicausal, with no particular beginning and no end. More a climate than an event, so not the way apocalypse stories liked to have a big event, after which everybody ran around with guns … or else were eaten alive by something caused by the big event.”

The idea of a world-ending cascade of crises can’t help but grip the imagination as bad headlines accumulate. It’s not just the tech failures, though there wereplentymoreof those. This week, the US also lost itsmeasleselimination status, as did Bolivia and Mexico. Parts of Florida were hit withsevere floodingafter more than a foot of rain. These developments followed the hottest summer on record — one marked by drought, wildfires and Britain’sworst cereal harvestin four decades.

“I think about William Gibson’s Jackpot coinage more than I’d prefer, lately,”anotherposter wrote.

Though the people living through Gibson’s jackpot had a vague sense that things were going horribly wrong, they didn’t quite comprehend the gravity: “No comets crashing, nothing you could really call a nuclear war. Just everything else, tangled in the changing climate: droughts, water shortages, crop failures, honeybees gone like they almost were now, collapse of other keystone species, every last alpha predator gone, antibiotics doing even less than they already did, diseases that were never quite the one big pandemic but big enough to be historic events in themselves. And all of it around people: how people were, how many of them there were, how they’d changed things just by being there.”

Gibson’s choice of the term “jackpot” has a few layers. The word was first recorded in the mid-19th century, describing a version of draw poker called Jack Pots — and the pool of chips that accumulated in the game until a player had good enough cards (a pair of jacks or better) to open the betting.

A jackpot today conjures images of a big, fat lottery payout; in a more figurative sense, “to hit the jackpot” is to enjoy an unexpected success or reward.

Read this way, Gibson’s “jackpot” is a dark joke — so many crises came together at once, like cards in a poker hand or symbols lining up on a slot machine, that contemporary civilization couldn’t withstand them all. In the aftermath, the 20% of people who survived hit a different kind of jackpot: a world of wealth and continued scientific and technological progress, with far fewer people who might want to share in it.

Jackpot can also mean a dilemma or a predicament, often used as part of a phrase “to get into a jackpot” (or, as immortalized bybaseball umpire Tom Hallionin a foul-mouthed argument with New York Mets manager Terry Collins, to have one’s “a** in the jackpot”).

This usage likewise came out of poker, referring to the difficulty of extricating oneself from a game once prize winnings have ballooned to a certain level. In this sense, Gibson’s “jackpot” might forewarn of a problem that modern society has gotten itself into and must confront.

So: Are the events of the past week, along with the ever-increasing pace of AI advancement and the accelerated warming of the planet, a sign that we’re in a “jackpot”?

“I think we could be in the midst of an ongoing slow unraveling, but frankly, we don’t know,” said Luke Kemp, a researcher of existential risk and author of “Goliath’s Curse: The History and Future of Societal Collapse.” “Most of the time, you can’t really tell until retrospectively.”

As in Gibson’s novel, civilizational collapses tend to unfold less dramatically than the cataclysmic, end-times narratives found in major world religions, Kemp said.

“Collapse is simply a fragmentation and contraction of different power structures, whether it’s the state, the economy, the military networks,” he said. “And when these fragment and contract, it’s a process which has benefits and costs, winners and losers, some of which can be quite quick or can take quite some time.”

Though people attribute the fall of major civilizations throughout history to causes such as drought, disease or invaders, Kemp said the reality is more complicated. The Roman Empire, for example, didn’t fall suddenly but underwent a series of collapses that transpired over centuries as the result of a number of protracted conflicts and forces, he added.

Similarly, Kemp said, modern society faces multiple, intersecting crises that are worsening each other — a phenomenon that disaster experts and historians call “polycrisis.”

The challenge, as he sees it, is that the modern world is extremely interconnected, fast-moving and complex. While this makes it more resilient against smaller shocks, a bigger shock could spread devastation across the entire system.

To Kemp, the events of the past week made clear just how fragile and vulnerable the global infrastructure is. The fact that Microsoft’s Outlook outage disrupted basic operations across so many institutions, companies and government agencies, for example, is a sign of the world’s critical dependence on a handful of corporations in Silicon Valley, which in turn raises concerns about the erosion of national sovereignty, he said.

Zachary Kallenborn, a researcher who studies global catastrophic risk, took a more cautious view. The recent outages and the disruptions, he said, were more reflective of our anxieties than they were of any existential risk. And while he said vulnerabilities in digital infrastructure do pose serious issues that merit addressing, whether they could lead to a civilizational collapse depended on one’s definition of the term.

“The challenge when we talk about some of these slow, boring collapses is that it’s so complex and so dependent on lots of different decisions that happen over a large period of time,” Kallenborn said. “And especially if we’re talking about the scale of global civilization as opposed to individual society, there’s some inherent resilience somewhat built into the system because we have various countries around the world that are more or less isolated, more or less connected.”

Even before the recent outages, Daniel Holz — an astrophysicist and chair of the Science and Security Board of the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists, which sets the Doomsday Clock — and his colleagues have been sounding the alarm about the enormous risks before us. Currently, the Doomsday Clock, a physical representation of the likelihood of human-driven global catastrophe, is set at85 seconds to midnight— the closest since its inception in 1947.

In the clock’s early days, “midnight” indicated the threat of nuclear war. But in today’s complex world, there are many different definitions of “midnight.” The board that sets the clock is made up of nuclear scientists, environmental experts and infectious disease specialists, all of whom are focused on different kinds of threats to humanity.

Holz is worried about all of it — including the possibility that a number of incremental shifts could be what brings about a civilizational level catastrophe.

“Part of the problem is there are probably many ‘midnights’ that we haven’t even thought about yet,” Holz said.

The flurry of outages occurring one right after another isn’t necessarily an indicator of something nefarious, he said. But it was a sign that the global infrastructure is in dire need of investment and attention.

And the fact that so many outages seemed to happen at once might wake people up to the serious vulnerabilities in our systems.

“We’re starting to see, you know, the edifice crumble, and it’s just the beginning,” Holz said. “This can turn into a real kind of avalanche, and we really need to get out ahead of that.”
